fields.frontExample: I felt awkward asking for help.
fields.meaning: Feeling uncomfortable or self-conscious in a social situation, especially when you are unsure what to say or do.
fields.nativePronunciation: /ˈɑːkwɚd/ or /ˈɔːkwɚd/. Stress the first syllable. Keep the second syllable weak, with an American r-colored vowel.
examples: I always feel awkward when I don’t know anyone at a party.
The conversation got awkward when they started arguing.
That was an awkward moment, but everyone eventually laughed about it.
She’s gotten less awkward in meetings as she’s become more confident.
fields.usageNote: Use feel awkward for social discomfort: I felt awkward asking for help. Embarrassed is more specific: you feel self-conscious about something, often something you did. Awkward can also describe something difficult to use or handle; it is not limited to social situations.
fields.spanishPronunciation: Keep the second syllable weak. Use an American r without tapping or trilling it as in Spanish. Do not add a vowel after the final d.

edits.after: Keep the second syllable weak. Use an American r without tapping or trilling it as in Spanish. Do not add a vowel after the final d.

previousEdits.before: La segunda sílaba es débil y la r no se vibra como una r española. No añadas una vocal después de la d final. Usa el IPA como referencia; una aproximación escrita no reproduce todos los sonidos.
incómodo / sentirse incómodo; en este contexto: Me sentí incómodo al pedir ayuda.

fields.meaning: Making you feel very tired or low on energy, especially mentally or emotionally.
fields.category: Adjective — the -ing form of the regular verb drain used as an adjective
fields.nativePronunciation: /ˈdreɪnɪŋ/. Stress the first syllable. In careful pronunciation, -ing ends in /ɪŋ/: keep the nasal /ŋ/ without adding a separate g sound.
examples: Dealing with constant complaints is emotionally draining.
Yesterday’s meeting was really draining.
This project has been draining lately, but we’re almost finished.
Working long hours without breaks can be physically and mentally draining.
fields.usageNote: Draining describes what causes the tiredness: The meeting was draining. Drained describes the person’s feeling: I felt drained after the meeting. Say I feel drained, not I feel draining, when you mean that you are exhausted.
alternatives: taking a lot out of me
fields.spanishPronunciation: The vowel /ɪ/ in -ing differs in quality from Spanish /i/, not just in length. End with the nasal /ŋ/ at the back of the mouth, without a separate hard g sound.

edits.after: The vowel /ɪ/ in -ing differs in quality from Spanish /i/, not just in length. End with the nasal /ŋ/ at the back of the mouth, without a separate hard g sound.

previousEdits.before: Empieza con /dr/ y el diptongo /eɪ/. En -ing, /ɪ/ no es la i española: cambia la posición de la lengua, no solo la duración. Termina con /ŋ/, sin añadir una g separada.
agotador / desgastante / que te deja sin energía (describe las reuniones que causan el cansancio).

fields.frontExample: I went to the office yesterday.
fields.meaning: Went is the past simple of go. Here, it means that I traveled to the office yesterday.
fields.nativePronunciation: /wɛnt/, one syllable; /ɛ/ is the vowel in bed. The forms sound different: go /ɡoʊ/, went /wɛnt/, gone /ɡɔn/ or /ɡɑːn/. Keep the final /nt/ together without adding a vowel; the t may be unreleased.
examples: I usually go to the gym after work.
We went out for dinner last night.
She’s already gone home.
He goes to the office early on Mondays.
fields.usageNote: In this example, went describes a completed trip: I went to the office yesterday. After have, has, or had, use gone, not went: She has gone home. After did or didn’t, use go: Did you go to the office?
fields.spanishPronunciation: Start with /w/ without adding a g before it. The vowel /ɛ/ is more open than Spanish /e/. Keep the final /nt/ cluster and do not add a vowel after t.

edits.after: Start with /w/ without adding a g before it. The vowel /ɛ/ is more open than Spanish /e/. Keep the final /nt/ cluster and do not add a vowel after t.

previousEdits.before: Empieza con /w/, sin añadir una g. La vocal /ɛ/ es más abierta que la e española. Conserva /nt/ al final y no añadas una e después de la t.
fui a la oficina (un viaje o desplazamiento ya terminado).

fields.frontExample: Let's not put off this conversation.
fields.meaning: To delay an activity or conversation until a later time, sometimes because you do not want to deal with it yet.
fields.nativePronunciation: /pʊt ˈɔf/ or /pʊt ˈɑf/. The base, past, and participle put sound the same. Link the final t into the vowel of off; phrase stress can vary with emphasis.
examples: I usually put off difficult tasks until the last minute.
I put off calling him yesterday because I didn’t know what to say.
We’ve put off the meeting until next week.
Don’t keep putting it off—you’ll have to do it eventually.
fields.usageNote: For another action, use -ing: put off calling him, not put off to call him. With a pronoun, say put it off, not put off it. With a noun, both put off the meeting and put the meeting off are natural.
fields.spanishPronunciation: Keep /ʊ/ relaxed; it differs in quality from Spanish /u/. Link put and off without inserting an extra vowel, and finish off with /f/.

edits.after: Keep /ʊ/ relaxed; it differs in quality from Spanish /u/. Link put and off without inserting an extra vowel, and finish off with /f/.

previousEdits.before: La vocal /ʊ/ de put es más relajada y diferente de la u española; no es solo una diferencia de duración. Une las palabras sin añadir una vocal entre ellas y conserva la f final de off.
posponer / aplazar / dejar para después; en este contexto: posponer esta conversación.

fields.meaning: To make something stronger or keep it going. Here, the rumors make the argument stronger or harder to stop.
fields.nativePronunciation: /ˈfjuːəl/. The first part sounds like few; move toward the weak vowel /ə/ before the final l. Some American speakers compress the syllables.
examples: The new evidence fueled the debate at work.
His angry comments only fueled the argument.
Social media posts can fuel rumors and unnecessary conflict.
The team’s recent success has fueled hopes for a championship.
fields.usageNote: Here, fuel is a verb: rumors fuel an argument by making it stronger. It is regular; the American past spelling is fueled, with one l: The announcement fueled speculation. As a noun, fuel means a substance used for energy: We need more fuel for the car.
fields.spanishPronunciation: Move smoothly from /f/ into the /j/ glide, as in English yes. Avoid replacing that glide with a strongly fricated consonant. Keep the second vowel /ə/ weak rather than turning it into a full open vowel.

edits.after: Move smoothly from /f/ into the /j/ glide, as in English yes. Avoid replacing that glide with a strongly fricated consonant. Keep the second vowel /ə/ weak rather than turning it into a full open vowel.

previousEdits.before: Empieza con /f/ seguida de /j/, como la y inglesa en yes, y luego /uː/. La segunda vocal /ə/ es débil: no la conviertas en una a española fuerte.
alimentar / avivar; en este contexto: Estos rumores alimentan la discusión.
